extracted.intended_audience: readers concerned about media consolidation: independent-media supporters, activists, journalists, and the general public
extracted.subtask_description: An opinion/feature piece arguing that a handful of corporations control the bulk of US mass media and urging antitrust action; describes indicators of dangerous consolidation and gives examples of corporate ownership across media sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration measured by number of dominant corporations
rubrics_metrics.description: The decline in the number of corporations dominating mass media over time (from 50 in 1983 to about six in the latest edition of The Media Monopoly) is presented as an indicator of dangerous concentration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use changes in the count of firms dominating most mass media as a metric of consolidation; the article cites Bagdikian's editions showing 50 (1983) → 29 (1987) → 23 (1990) → 14 (1992) → 10 (1997) → ~6 (2000) to illustrate steep, ominous trend lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership of major broadcast television networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a conglomerate owns national broadcast networks (CBS, NBC, ABC, Fox) is a key sign of its influence over public discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: CBS merged with Viacom; NBC is owned by General Electric; ABC is owned by Disney; Fox is owned by News Corp. If a firm owns a major network, chances are slim it will invite discussion critical of its own industry practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of cable news and cable channels by conglomerates
rubrics_metrics.description: Conglomerate ownership of cable news channels concentrates control of televised news and reduces the likelihood of critical coverage of media concentration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: CNN (Time Warner), CNBC (General Electric), MSNBC (GE/Microsoft venture), Fox News Channel (News Corp). The article argues that because these channels are owned by Big Six firms, antitrust talk is unlikely on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominance in book publishing and cross-media holdings
rubrics_metrics.description: Ownership of major book publishers and broad cross-media holdings magnify a conglomerate's cultural and political influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Bertelsmann (owner of Random House) is cited as 'the world's third largest conglomerate' with holdings in magazines, newspapers, music, television, online trading, films, and radio in many countries — making it difficult to publish or promote critiques of consolidation within its channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertical integration with major internet service providers/portals
rubrics_metrics.description: When dominant media firms merge with major ISPs/portals (e.g., AOL + Time Warner), they gain power to shape online visibility and gatekeep information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AOL Time Warner is used as an example: as a dominant ISP/portal it can highlight corporate-friendly links and steer subscriber attention, reducing the internet's role as an independent public sphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocks, cross-ownership, and joint ventures among conglomerates
rubrics_metrics.description: Interlocking ownership, stock stakes in one another, and cooperative joint ventures among the dominant firms reinforce consolidated power across media sectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bagdikian's point (quoted) that the firms are 'intertwined: they own stock in each other, they cooperate in joint media ventures' is cited to explain how such interconnections amplify influence beyond a simple headcount of firms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercialization and corporate-friendly curation of online content
rubrics_metrics.description: The commercialization of high-traffic websites and corporate control over curated links/contents tends to produce overwhelmingly corporate-friendly online environments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes AOL's tendency to 'highlight' its parent firm's offerings and more generally describes cyberspace as increasingly commercialized and organized as a 'virtual cul-de-sac' rather than an open forum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likelihood that mainstream outlets will host antitrust critics
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical criterion for assessing media openness: whether major outlets owned by conglomerates will invite critics of media consolidation to speak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author rhetorically assesses each major broadcast network and concludes that invitations to critics like Bagdikian to discuss vigorous antitrust enforcement are unlikely on these outlets because of ownership ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for organized antitrust movement to change corporate indifference
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence or absence of a strong antitrust movement is treated as a decisive factor for forcing change in media consolidation practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece argues that only a strong antitrust movement aimed at the Big Six could quickly alter the firms' indifference to public concerns; this is presented as the recommended remedy rather than a descriptive metric.
